response: The authors describe a systematic review methodology that assembles, filters, and categorises literature corpora for this survey, emphasizing coverage, transparency, volume management, and reproducibility. Figure 4 shows the corpora composition: the principal RFM‑related “main” corpus (81.2 % of 1 263 publications), an “implications” corpus (9.9 %), and a “further” supplementary set (8.9 %). The section outlines the automated acquisition pipeline, filtering strategies, post‑processing steps, and criteria guiding each corpus’s composition and role in the review.

Robotic foundation models (RFMs) show promise for instruction‑ and demonstration‑driven control, yet their industrial applicability remains under‑investigated. This survey maps the RFM landscape, linking industrial domains and use cases to requirements—especially for collaborative robots, heterogeneous sensing/actuation, edge‑computing limits, and safety‑critical operation. Eleven interdependent implications are distilled into an assessment framework of 149 criteria covering model capabilities and ecosystem needs. Applying the framework, 324 manipulation‑capable RFMs were evaluated via 48,276 LLM‑assisted, expert‑validated decisions. Results reveal limited, uneven industrial maturity: even top models meet only a fraction of criteria and show narrow, implication‑specific strengths rather than broad coverage. The authors conclude that advancing industry‑grade RFMs requires systematic integration of safety, real‑time feasibility, robust perception, interaction, and cost‑effective, auditable system integration, not isolated benchmark gains.

The authors created a modular Python pipeline (DB‑Search) to automate literature acquisition while keeping manual effort limited to “Manual Refinement” steps. Users supply one or more structured Academic Search Query Syntax (ASQS) queries, a publication‑date range (e.g., 2020‑present), chosen databases (arXiv, GoogleScholar, OpenAlex, Scopus, SemanticScholar), a retrieval‑preference (latest vs. most relevant), and optional upper bounds on results per DB‑query pair (e.g., 100). The system translates each ASQS query into the native syntax of each target DB, relaxes unsupported features, and scans all DB‑query permutations. Metadata from APIs is merged; duplicates are removed using identifiers such as DOIs, missing metadata is fetched from auxiliary APIs, and validity checks (e.g., title‑abstract consistency) exclude articles with errors or insufficient identifiers. A second duplicate‑removal pass follows these checks. Validated articles are saved as JSON/YAML (optionally PDF) with detailed fields and auto‑generated reports describing queries, time spans, database selections, result counts, timestamps, and per‑DB‑query statistics. An on‑demand LLM‑based filter (GPT‑4o) scores semantic relevance, providing a binary label, a score in [0, 1], and a brief justification; filtering can be staged with increasingly strict criteria. A “Query Proposal” component (two GPT‑4o instances) generates initial query suggestions from the ASQS definition and user intent to support iterative refinement. After automated retrieval, manual post‑processing (enrichment, correction, additional filters) is applied to ensure quality, completeness, and relevance. No explicit author‑stated limitations are reported for this section.

The authors describe robotic foundation models (RFMs) as data‑driven, highly adaptable systems that extend the foundation‑model paradigm from language and vision to robotics. They note that foundation models (FMs) are trained on large, heterogeneous datasets, often with self‑supervised objectives, and can exhibit emergent behaviours that exceed their explicit training goals. When applied to robotics, additional challenges arise because robot actions form high‑dimensional, closed‑loop decision processes that continuously affect sensory feedback, and robotic platforms vary widely in embodiment, configuration, and operational context. Classical control methods are typically deterministic, task‑specific, and lack generalisability, motivating the need for task‑agnostic, cross‑embodiment, open‑ended control approaches.

The authors define RFMs as models that possess a “generalist core” enabling efficient adaptation to new tasks, settings, embodiments, and hardware with minimal engineering or retraining, such as through high‑level instructions or flexible action representations. To qualify, an RFM must provide (1) multi‑modality—ingestion of proprioceptive, exteroceptive, image, and natural‑language signals; (2) output flexibility—generation of actions, plans, trajectories, or similar outputs for diverse robots and domains; and (3) adaptability—ability to generalise or adapt to novel tasks, environments, or embodiments with little manual intervention. Models lacking these properties are deemed specialised or narrow rather than true RFMs.

The paper distinguishes “single‑purpose” RFMs (focused on a single capability such as perception, planning, or control) from “general‑purpose” RFMs that span multiple functions, arguing that only the latter truly qualify. Vision‑Language‑Action models (VLAs) are treated as a distinct sub‑category of RFMs: they employ multimodal inputs (language and vision) to enable human‑like instructability and generate low‑level robot actions, aligning with the RFM criteria of multimodality and output flexibility. VLAs typically consist of perception, reasoning/planning, and action modules, though the authors accept models without strict modular separation. VLAs also bridge digital and embodied AI, requiring robustness to real‑world complexity and hardware constraints.

RFMs are further categorised by primary function: (a) RFMs for control, which directly output low‑level motor commands, joint velocities, or force/torque signals across varied embodiments; (b) RFMs for planning, which produce high‑level reasoning, task decomposition, or sequential plans for downstream controllers; and (c) integrated RFMs that combine planning and control, representing a step toward general‑purpose robotic intelligence with internal reasoning, failure explanation, and long‑horizon planning. The authors note that planners align closely with the RFM paradigm because their outputs are high‑level.

Beyond VLAs, other multimodal or non‑language models (e.g., Vision‑Action models such as DP or Dreamitate) can qualify as RFMs if they exhibit multi‑purpose adaptability and support diverse tasks or embodiments. Specialized subclasses target domains like manipulation, locomotion, navigation, aerial, underwater, or mobile‑manipulation robotics; manipulation is highlighted as especially relevant for industrial use. Ultimately, the survey’s inclusion criterion is that a model must demonstrate cross‑task or cross‑embodiment adaptability, multimodal input integration, and flexible output generation to be considered an RFM.

The introduction frames industrial robotics as shifting from tightly‑engineered, isolated automation toward flexible, collaborative deployment, driven by the rise of collaborative robots (cobots) that must be commissioned quickly, redeployed across changing processes, and operate near humans. Although cobots retain high mechanical precision and low power use, their industrial usefulness is now limited more by the availability of robust, adaptive, and intuitive control methods than by actuation performance. This motivates renewed focus on learning‑based robot intelligence that can handle variability in tasks, environments, actuation, and sensing while meeting industrial constraints such as safety, reliability, low‑latency operation, and cost‑effective integration.

Recent advances in large‑scale learning have produced Foundation Models (FMs), which aim to reduce manual engineering by transferring knowledge across tasks—an attractive prospect for high‑mix, low‑volume industrial settings. Robotic Foundation Models (RFMs) extend this idea to embodied decision‑making, providing a flexible platform for transferring across tasks, interfaces, and embodiments. The survey concentrates on RFMs that generate low‑level actions for direct robot actuation, because this interface is central to real‑world deployment and tightly coupled to industrial constraints (latency, safety gating, hardware‑specific action spaces). While many architectural approaches exist (diffusion‑based, dreaming‑based, dual‑system designs), the authors deliberately omit an architectural taxonomy, referring readers elsewhere for that coverage.

To connect methodological progress to practical deployment, the authors propose a hierarchical categorisation of robotic control methods (Figure 1): (1) Predefined/Rule‑based—fixed trajectories lacking dynamic adaptation; (2) Reactive/Parametrised—sensor‑driven limited adaptation; (3) Specialised/Narrow—task‑specific solutions; (4) Foundational—broadly pretrained systems enabling efficient fine‑tuning; (5) Generalist—zero‑shot or in‑context generalisation with only high‑level instructions or online demonstration. This hierarchy illustrates a trajectory from rigid, task‑specific automation toward adaptable, instruction‑driven operation with reduced commissioning effort.

The authors note that the introduction of FMs marks a transition from specialised control (level 3) to foundational robotics (level 4), yet this does not automatically yield industry‑grade autonomy. Achieving true generalist capability (level 5) requires robust online adaptation, dependable instruction following, and safe operation under uncertainty—critical in dynamic, cost‑driven industrial environments. Publication counts for RFMs and related work have risen sharply, especially in 2025, risking fragmentation and inflated claims without structured industrial evaluation. Existing surveys lack a systematic, implication‑grounded assessment of industrial deployment readiness, prompting this review.

The survey’s structure links foundational concepts to industrial requirements and then to a systematic assessment of current RFMs. After defining RFMs and positioning them within the control hierarchy (Section 2), the authors describe their review methodology and corpus composition (Section 3), discuss related works (Section 4), and provide background on cobot adoption and hardware, sensing, and edge‑computing constraints (Sections 5‑6). Section 7 distils industrial deployment viewpoints into eleven interdependent implications and operationalises them into a 149‑item criteria catalogue for assessing industrial maturity. Section 8 applies this framework to manipulation‑capable RFMs, presenting an overview and criteria‑based maturity evaluation; Section 9 synthesises findings.

A preview of results indicates that, despite impressive benchmark progress and broader contributions, industrial maturity remains limited and uneven: current models typically address only a few enabling dimensions rather than providing integrated coverage of deployment‑critical requirements. This motivates the primary goal of moving discussion from isolated benchmark successes toward a traceable, implication‑grounded view of what constitutes a credible industrial RFM. The authors’ main contributions are: (1) the control‑method categorisation; (2) a concrete definition and clustering of RFMs; (3) a comprehensive overview of manipulation‑capable RFMs; (4) an industrial perspective on cobot rise; (5) synthesis of domain‑agnostic industrial implications; (6) the 149‑item criteria catalogue; and (7) a large‑scale evaluation of the RFM landscape against this catalogue, highlighting strengths, weaknesses, and research gaps needed for industry‑grade RFMs.

The authors built a principal RFM‑related literature corpus to cover all major research directions on robotic foundation models (RFMs) and adjacent topics such as training protocols, extensions, applications, safety, robustness and adversarial challenges. They excluded LLM‑based high‑level or narrowly specialised approaches, grouping those separately as “High‑Level”. Using a standardized Python pipeline (Section 3.1), they performed two large‑scale retrievals (identical parameters) on 4 July 2025 (10 728 valid entries, 5 035 unique) and 30 Oct 2025 (12 027 valid entries, 4 999 unique). After merging and a cautious duplicate‑removal protocol, 6 497 unique classified articles remained. A coarse LLM filter removed non‑robotics papers, retaining 4 834; a stricter LLM filter for RFM relevance yielded 1 408 articles, with no false‑negative cases identified in manual cross‑checks. Manual in‑depth review, enrichment and manual duplicate discarding produced a final categorized corpus of 1 025 unique, highly relevant works. This corpus comprises 341 control or integrated RFMs (324 for manipulation‑related domains, 17 for other embodiments), 321 related works (e.g., training protocols, extensions), 231 High‑Level articles (LLM‑based or narrowly scoped models), 77 data/benchmark articles, and 55 surveys/reviews (24 general embodied AI, 31 including RFMs, 11 focused on RFMs, only 2 on industrial relevance). The resulting set serves as the reference for all subsequent review analyses, ensuring broad and systematic coverage of RFMs and closely associated fields.

The authors built an industrial implication corpus to capture requirements, challenges, and context‑specific attributes of real‑world robotic applications. Using the modular literature pipeline from Section 3.1, they issued seven broad ASQS queries (Table B3) covering applications, case studies, analyses, and reviews, limited to publications from 2015 to July 2025 across arXiv, GoogleScholar, OpenAlex, Scopus, and SemanticScholar, retrieving up to 50 results per query (max 1,750). The search returned 1,240 valid entries, of which 892 were unique after deduplication. A coarse LLM‑based relevance filter (same intent as the original search) reduced the set to 296 relevant and 596 unrelated articles. The authors then manually reviewed the 125 most relevant articles (LLM relevance ≥ 0.9), deeming this subset sufficient for extracting industrial implications, which are later synthesized and mapped to the RFM paradigm (Section 7).

The authors performed additional automated and manual searches covering industrial robots, cobots, compute hardware, sensors, manipulators, efficiency considerations, related fields, and norms/standards, which yielded 113 auxiliary publications that were considered and used throughout the development of the work.

The authors define Robotic Foundation Models (RFMs) as highly adaptable, data‑driven systems that must exhibit a generalist core—cross‑task and cross‑embodiment adaptability—while ingesting multimodal proprioceptive, exteroceptive, and language inputs and producing flexible outputs such as actions, plans, or trajectories; they distinguish RFMs from single‑purpose models and view Vision‑Language‑Action models as a prominent sub‑category that meets these criteria, and they further categorize RFMs into control‑focused, planning‑focused, and integrated models, noting that specialization (e.g., manipulation‑only) lacks the required generalism.

The introduction notes that industrial robotics is shifting from highly optimized, isolated automation toward flexible, collaborative cobot deployment, making robust, adaptive control—especially learning‑based robotic foundation models (RFMs) that generate low‑level actions—more critical than raw actuation performance; it outlines a control‑method hierarchy (predefined → reactive → specialised → foundational → generalist) to frame RFMs’ evolution and argues that despite rapid publication growth, current RFMs show limited, uneven industrial maturity, addressing only few deployment‑critical dimensions, which motivates the survey’s goal to assess and guide progress toward truly industry‑grade, generalist systems.

source_label: Section: 5 Rise of Cobots in Industry
response: Recent advances in RFMs are mainly demonstrated together with cobots, but these developments are often confined to laboratory, table‑top, or kitchen environments; the authors note that highlighting the broader industrial significance requires first examining the evolution of industrial robotics and the shift toward more collaborative robotic systems.

The authors conducted an extensive literature review (Section 3.2) and identified 55 survey and review articles relevant to embodied AI. Figure 9 shows that the corpus comprises surveys covering general embodied AI (GEA), those that include robot‑foundation models (+RFMs), and those with an explicit industrial focus (IND). Of the 55 surveys, 11 (20 %) specifically target the robot‑foundation model (RFM) field, yet none of these present an explicit industrial focus and almost all centre on vision‑language agents (VLAs), which constitute only one subset of RFMs. Only two surveys (3.6 % of the total) have a clear industrial application focus: Fan et al. [35] concentrates on vision‑language models for human‑robot collaboration in smart manufacturing, and Ren et al. [36] discusses general embodied intelligence in industrial contexts without addressing specific model classes. Consequently, the literature lacks a dedicated survey on industrial applications of RFMs, and virtually no attention has been given to RFM sub‑categories such as vision‑action or other control‑oriented integrated RFMs (Section 2). The authors therefore position their work to fill this gap: beyond the prevailing emphasis on VLA architectures and functionalities, they provide a taxonomy‑driven, extensive overview of the broader RFM landscape and a detailed analysis of the attributes and capabilities required by industrial use cases. This analysis aims to inform future RFM design and to propose criteria for evaluating industrial maturity—perspectives that are currently unmet in existing surveys.

The authors expanded their literature base beyond the two primary corpora by conducting both automated and manual searches that targeted industrial robots, collaborative robots, computing hardware, sensors, manipulators, efficiency considerations, related fields, and applicable norms and standards. This broader search yielded 113 auxiliary publications. All of these additional sources were incorporated into the authors’ workflow and informed the development and writing of the present study.

source_label: Section: 5 Rise of Cobots in Industry
response: The authors note that recent advances in robotic force‑modulation (RFM) technologies are mainly shown together with collaborative robots (cobots), but these demonstrations are often limited to laboratory, table‑top, or kitchen environments. They argue that to appreciate the wider industrial relevance of this trend, it is necessary first to review how industrial robotics has evolved and how it is moving toward increasingly collaborative robotic systems.

source_label: Section: 5.1 Landscape of Industrial Robotics: Tradition & Transformation
response: Industrial robots are defined as automatically controlled, reprogrammable multipurpose manipulators with three or more axes, requiring additional tooling (e.g., grippers, welding torches) and featuring complex kinematic chains that give mobility across many processes. They are typically programmed for predefined functions, need specialised expertise for reprogramming, operate at high speeds with large payloads, and are placed in separate spaces from humans for safety, serving heavy‑duty, repetitive or hazardous tasks. Configurations include six categories—Delta (parallel, symmetric PPP chains, high speed/acceleration, redundancy), Cartesian (serial PPP, smooth linear motion, rectangular workspace), Cylindrical (serial RPP, cylindrical workspace, revolute joints on same axis), SCARA (serial RRP, high accuracy, planar positioning), Spherical (serial RRR/RRP, simplified collision analysis, spherical workspace), and Articulated (serial RRR, human‑arm‑like, flexible 3D workspace). Traditional types lack flexibility, adaptability, safe direct human‑robot collaboration (HRC) and interaction (HRI), which modern manufacturing—especially SMEs—now demand. Cobots arose to address these limits: initially passive devices for guided movement, they have evolved into articulated robots designed for safe, efficient coexistence with humans. They feature lower payloads, reduced speeds, rounded shapes and sensor suites for real‑time contact or human detection, enabling intentional HRC. Cobots emphasize flexible deployment, intuitive HRI, easy programming, rapid reconfiguration, low downtime and cost, supporting high product variability and small batch sizes. Their functional ethos differs from traditional robots: rather than replacing humans in isolated environments, cobots aim to augment human capability, enabling joint execution of complex, variable, or ergonomically challenging tasks, prioritising safety, integration ease and shared‑workflow efficiency over maximal speed or payload.

The authors report that, beyond the two primary corpora described earlier, they conducted further automated and manual searches covering a range of topics—including industrial robots, collaborative robots (cobots), computing hardware, sensors, manipulators, efficiency considerations, additional related fields, and relevant norms and standards. These searches yielded a total of 113 auxiliary publications. The authors state that all of these auxiliary sources were taken into account and incorporated throughout the process of developing and writing the present work.

The authors note that cobots, while useful for supplementing human labor on routine or ergonomic tasks, still cannot autonomously manage complex, cognitive, or dexterous processes and face challenges in real‑time hazard detection, continuous safe operation, and trustworthy HRI/HRC. Trust and transparency are identified as critical success factors for cobot deployment. They propose that RFMs, integrated into cobot platforms, could address these challenges by enabling intuitive instruction, autonomous decision‑making, and real‑time adaptation via natural‑language input, multisensor fusion, and advanced reasoning. The authors stress that future work must ensure RFMs are robust beyond controlled labs, functioning effectively in the variable, safety‑critical environments of real industry, and that assessing RFMs’ industrial applicability is essential.

Modern cobots, noted for greater flexibility and safety than traditional industrial robots, have moved beyond laboratory demos to become integral across diverse real‑world domains. In manufacturing and assembly they are frequently used for precision‑adaptable tasks such as assembly, pick‑and‑place, machine tending, quality inspection, palletising, packaging, material handling and welding/gluing, with concrete examples like Universal Robots’ UR10e at PSA and Fiat Chrysler for door, hood and soft‑top assembly, riveting and mounting, as well as repetitive pick‑and‑place in plant nurseries, board‑manufacturing packaging and metal‑working soldering, drilling and arc‑welding. In quality control and inspection, cobots equipped with advanced sensors and computer‑vision perform real‑time dimension, integrity and defect checks, exemplified by UR3s inspecting automotive touchscreen panels. Integrated with Autonomous Mobile Robots, cobot arms form mobile manipulators that transport goods, feed machines and support agile, just‑in‑time logistics, illustrated by MiR200 AMRs moving assembly components in appliance manufacturing and handling heavy, repetitive, ergonomically challenging transports. Healthcare applications include patient handling, rehabilitation, medication dispensing and precise surgical assistance such as tool manipulation and remote ultrasound/endoscope positioning. In agriculture, cobots execute precise planting, harvesting and sorting, enabling continuous 24/7 operation to lessen seasonal manual labour. Retail and service uses involve shelf stocking, object retrieval and customer engagement to boost service quality and efficiency. Military, security and inspection deployments employ sensor‑equipped cobots for luggage scanning, hazardous substance detection, bomb disposal, facility inspection, cleaning and delicate manipulation, including surface inspection/cleaning of the Space Rider orbiter, bomb defusing with specialised tools and border‑inspection assistance.

source_label: Section: 5.3 Drivers of the Industrial Shift Toward Cobots
response: The authors report a shift in industry from manual labour and traditional industrial robots toward cobots, driven by technological, organisational and economic factors that demand adaptable, user‑friendly automation. Traditional robots are high‑payload, precise and fast but are complex, costly and hard to reconfigure, making them unsuitable for SMEs focused on low‑volume, high‑mix production. Cobots address these needs with flexible design, compact footprint and easy programming, offering intuitive interfaces that reduce reliance on specialised engineering and shorten integration time. They are intended to assist humans by taking repetitive, physically demanding or hazardous tasks, enhancing safety and allowing workers to focus on cognitive work. Their design enables direct human‑robot collaboration, combining human creativity with robotic reliability, supported by safety features such as real‑time sensors, force/torque monitoring and adaptive behaviour, which lessen the need for cages. Research and practice show rising cobot demand: a survey found a >5‑fold increase in cobot‑focused publications over a decade, and global installations grew from 11 000 units in 2017 to 55 000 in 2022. The International Federation of Robotics notes a growing proportion of cobots relative to traditional robots. Advances in computer vision and adaptive control extend cobot capabilities, aligning with Industry 4.0 goals of flexible, autonomous, and connected smart factories.

The authors argue that assessing RFMs for industry requires understanding cobot capabilities (reach, payload, accuracy, perception, manipulation) and practical hardware factors such as power consumption and inference hardware, which are often omitted in scientific studies. They outline that this section reviews key hardware and system components for industrial cobot deployment, presenting quantitative cobot capabilities and power profiles (6.1), industrial edge computing characteristics for real‑time control and inference (6.3), and essential sensing and manipulation hardware (6.2). Using survey data and representative hardware comparisons, they aim to clarify technical prerequisites for integrating RFMs in cobotic settings, covering robot capability, computational infrastructure, sensor integration and operational efficiency.

The authors note that industrial deployment settings differ from labs, combining heterogeneous hardware, strict safety and compliance, high reliability targets, and continuous operational pressures. They outline a three‑step analysis: (1) synthesize the industrial implication corpus into eleven general, domain‑agnostic requirements for robotics applications; (2) translate these implications into structured attributes to discuss how constraints appear in RFMs and their ecosystem; (3) consolidate the attributes into a criteria catalogue for consistent, transparent evaluation of industrial maturity across existing RFMs.

Sensors are essential for cobot perception and self‑monitoring, supporting HRC, HRI, autonomous navigation, manipulation and real‑time task execution. Commonly deployed types include visual (RGB, depth, CCD, 2D/3D vision), range (LiDAR, RADAR, sonar, ultrasonic, TOF/PMD, laser scanners), dynamics (IMUs, gyroscopes, accelerometers, force/torque, tactile, pressure), position/identification (encoders, RFID, infrared, GPS, odometry, magnetic), and specialised (acoustic, thermal) sensors. Advanced RFMs benefit from sensor fusion—e.g., vision with proximity, inertial or force/torque data—to improve robustness, safety and compliance, often using redundant or complementary modalities such as visual‑tactile feedback or force sensing for contact detection. End‑effectors (grippers, suction cups, dual‑stage tools, custom drills/polishers) are task‑specific, frequently embed sensors (force feedback, vision) and are modular for rapid adaptation, assuming compatible control‑algorithm flexibility. The extensive sensing and manipulation hardware expands observation‑action permutations, underscoring the need for multimodal, flexible outputs in modern control algorithms, a core requirement of RFMs.

The authors surveyed articulated anthropomorphic cobots using data from Taesi et al. [50], summarising 180 models (Table 4) and 63 models with payloads 0.5–20 kg (Table 5). Reported statistics show a mean of 6.09 DOFs (median 6), mean payload 8.56 kg (median 5.5 kg), mean reach 970 mm (median 910 mm) and positioning accuracy mean 0.09 mm (median 0.05 mm). Extreme outliers (e.g., 170 kg payload, 2790 mm reach) raise the means but most cobots handle moderate loads with high repeatability. For the 0.5–20 kg subset, TCP velocity ranges 0.2–6 m s⁻¹ (mean 1.68 m s⁻¹, median 1.1 m s⁻¹) and power consumption ranges 0.06–0.9 kW (mean 0.31 kW, median 0.25 kW). These power levels are far lower than conventional industrial robots (≈3 kW average, peaks up to 12–15 kW). The authors argue that cobots’ modest energy demand supports deployment in low‑power, mobile, or battery‑powered settings and influences hardware and computational choices for real‑time, low‑latency inference under constrained power budgets.

The authors extended the eleven industrial implications identified in Section 7.1 into a structured set of deployment‑relevant attributes to clarify how industry expectations (e.g., safe collaboration, robustness under uncertainty, real‑time feasibility) could manifest in RFM‑based systems. They derived 47 attributes covering hardware, tasks, environment, objects/materials, instructability, distractors, adaptability, online adaptation, internal interfaces, ID/OOD robustness, adversarial robustness, authorisation, security, detection/recognition, multimodal inputs/outputs, integration, safety, compliance, supervision, fault tolerance, reasoning/intention, model feedback, external guidance, interaction, and additional categories such as precision, trust, goal specification, solution strategy, offline adaptation, energy, data inference frequency, documentation, self‑awareness, memory, anomaly correction, and repeatability. An iterative mapping paired each implication with every attribute, producing 517 implication‑attribute cells that capture industrial concerns and constraints for RFM development and deployment. This matrix‑based approach highlights inter‑dependencies among implications (e.g., safety with perception, real‑time feasibility with interaction) and aims to reduce under‑representation of requirements. The resulting attribute set serves as a compact intermediate representation that informs the criteria catalogue (Section 7.3) and underpins an assessment framework for evaluating industrial readiness of existing RFMs. The full matrix is not reproduced due to size.

The authors explain that cobotic applications demand low‑latency, real‑time AI control, so computational platforms are typically deployed as edge devices placed as close as possible to the robot and its sensors, often integrated into the cobot controller. Edge devices process data locally, avoiding reliance on cloud or external datacentres, which is crucial for latency‑sensitive, mobile or remote robotics where network traffic must be minimized. Alternative paradigms such as fog or cloud computing can supply scalable resources but require additional infrastructure, non‑local hardware, stable networking, and incur higher latency, lower throughput, and greater risk of service interruption, making them less suitable for time‑critical robotic control. The authors note that moving computation toward the edge is increasingly important for industrial deployments because compute costs are dropping and recurring networking expenses are reduced.

To clarify hardware requirements for industrial robotic force‑motion (RFM) deployment, the authors present an overview of currently available edge devices and conduct a quantitative hardware analysis (Table 6). They select NVIDIA as the representative manufacturer because Jetson devices are widely adopted in robotics research and industry, offering a standardized, scalable portfolio (Nano to Thor series) with consistently documented performance metrics, pricing, and specifications, enabling accurate, fair, and reproducible comparisons of hardware suitability for modern AI‑based robotic control methods. While the table focuses on the Jetson portfolio, the authors acknowledge that other manufacturers (Siemens, AMD/Xilinx, Intel, Advantech, Beckhoff, etc.) also provide relevant edge devices, but comparable up‑to‑date public data for many of these alternatives are limited or unavailable.

Table 6 lists price, INT8 TOPS, memory, power, and derived efficiency metrics (e.g., TOPS per dollar, TOPS per watt, memory per dollar, annual operational cost) for each Jetson model and for a desktop‑class RTX 5090 GPU used as a reference point for the upper bound of single‑device computational performance. Prices reflect single‑unit purchases from the same NVIDIA‑specified retailer on the same date; operational costs assume 24/7 usage at $0.25 /kWh. The RTX 5090 is not an edge device but serves to illustrate trade‑offs between workstation‑grade and edge‑class hardware.

From the comparative statistics the authors identify several trends. The Orin Nano series offers the lowest entry cost and high performance relative to price, making it suitable for cost‑sensitive or large‑scale deployments. The entry‑level Xavier NX, despite being more expensive, provides the lowest overall AI compute performance in the lineup, but its 8 GB variant has the lowest maximum power consumption, favoring applications where minimal energy draw is essential. Mid‑tier devices such as the Orin AGX 32 GB balance increased computational capability with moderate power requirements and emerge as the most efficient in terms of compute power per operational cost, offering a strong compromise for applications prioritising both capability and efficiency. High‑end devices (Jetson Thor series or workstation GPUs) deliver substantially higher throughput but incur markedly higher energy consumption and annual operational costs, limiting scalability for mobile, battery‑powered, or energy‑constrained platforms. The RTX 5090 can consume more than twice the power of a median cobot, underscoring that desktop GPUs target short, intensive workloads in energy‑abundant environments, whereas edge devices are optimized for consistent, energy‑efficient operation in resource‑constrained settings.

The authors conclude that deploying larger, more capable RFMs is constrained by both compute and energy efficiency considerations, highlighting the need to align model design with operational cost and industrial practicality. They also note that industrial‑class (IND) devices often include features such as ECC memory for increased reliability, which can raise both initial and operational expenses or reduce computational power compared with standard research hardware.

The authors surveyed 324 manipulation‑capable RFMs, evaluating each against 149 implication‑grounded criteria (48,276 decisions) to produce overall maturity scores and implication‑wise profiles (Section 8.1). They detail the scalable evaluation methodology, design choices, and an agreement/consistency check with expert judgments on a small ground‑truth subset. Results include a summary of the strongest‑performing RFMs (Section 8.2) and an industrial applicability analysis for the full corpus and the Top‑50 subset (Section 8.3), which together characterize current industrial maturity, highlight well‑ and poorly‑addressed implications, and provide a baseline for the synthesis and outlook in Section 9.

The authors note that cobotic applications demand low‑latency, real‑time AI processing on edge devices placed near robots to avoid cloud‑induced delays, and they therefore review representative industrial edge PCs, focusing on NVIDIA Jetson models because their performance, pricing and specifications are publicly documented and comparable. Using Table 6 they compare price, INT8 TOPS, memory, power and derived cost‑efficiency metrics, finding the Orin Nano offers the best performance‑per‑dollar, the Xavier NX the lowest power draw, the Orin AGX 32 GB the highest compute‑per‑operational‑cost efficiency, while high‑end Thor series and RTX 5090 deliver greater throughput at substantially higher energy and annual costs. They conclude that selecting RFMs for industrial deployment must balance computational capability with power consumption and operational expense, noting that industrial‑class (IND) devices may add ECC‑memory reliability at further cost.

source_label: Section: 7.3 Evaluating Industrial Maturity: A Criteria Catalogue
response:
The authors note that the eleven industrial implications identified in Section 7.1 describe recurring demands on deployed robotic systems, but that for robotic foundation models (RFMs) these demands must be expressed concretely in terms of model capabilities, interfaces, and the surrounding deployment stack. Building on the 517 implication‑attribute combinations from Section 7.2, they translated the implication‑grounded requirements into an explicit criteria catalogue intended to reason about, compare, and ultimately rate the industrial readiness of existing and future RFMs. For each implication‑attribute pair they collected and refined key deployment questions (e.g., behavior under distribution shifts, failure detection and handling, interpretation and verification of human input, required artefacts for audit and integration) and iteratively consolidated them into 149 criteria (C) spanning all eleven general industrial implications (I), listed in Appendix Table C4. The catalogue is presented as a living foundation that can be extended as additional industrial constraints or regulatory expectations emerge.

The scope of the criteria covers both RFMs and their deployment ecosystem. While most criteria target the model directly, the authors emphasize that industrial readiness also depends on the robot software stack, interfaces, safety infrastructure, monitoring, logging, and documentation. Accordingly, the catalogue includes criteria that are (a) primarily RFM‑centric (e.g., adaptive behavior under changing observations/actions), (b) primarily ecosystem‑centric (e.g., accessible documentation on training‑data composition and transfer behavior), or (c) require joint support (e.g., a model producing structured signals that can be persistently logged and leveraged by the surrounding system).

Because the industrial implications are inter‑dependent, the authors deliberately retain redundancy across implications. Criteria that appear under multiple implications are kept separate when the emphasis differs—for example, hot‑swapping appears under adaptability (I1‑C2), integration/cost (I7‑C4), and perception (I9‑C12), each stressing a distinct industrial concern. This redundancy preserves the ability to diagnose immaturity in a specific industrial dimension rather than concluding a generic lack of hot‑swapping support.

The catalogue reflects several key paradigms that are rarely discussed jointly in prior work and are often not yet implemented in current RFMs, though many are already investigated as distinct research directions. Central motifs include multi‑hardware support, hot‑swapping, and dimensionality adaptation through changing observation and action interfaces; robustness to out‑of‑distribution (OOD) scenarios, adversarial attacks, and anomalies; confidence calibration and uncertainty quantification; interactive clarification and feedback for human‑robot interaction; decoupled supervisory or verification layers for safety gating; and memory, data governance, and documentation. The authors cite recent work on unified action representations and adaptable architectures for new embodiments, runtime resilience to interface changes, online detection and fallback behavior, security weaknesses inherited from LLMs/VLMs, anomaly prediction via outcome forecasting, confidence calibration for uncertainty‑driven help‑seeking, linguistic ambiguity resolution with follow‑up questions, operator‑in‑the‑loop trajectory correction, reactive/proactive failure detection, memory modules that improve long‑horizon performance, privacy‑preserving training, and dataset construction that incorporates failures and recoveries. These studies substantiate the inclusion of corresponding criteria such as online detection, threat/attack detection, explicit recovery pathways, calibrated confidence signals, interactive supervision, redundant safety mechanisms, fault categorisation, persistent logging, memory mechanisms, data composition variation, transparency, privacy compliance, and learning from incidents.

The authors conclude that many catalogue requirements correspond to active research directions; the industrial immaturity of RFMs stems less from the absence of isolated technical proposals than from the lack of their systematic combination into a deployable, auditable, and safety‑governed ecosystem. The criteria catalogue therefore consolidates partially disconnected strands into a unified, implication‑grounded assessment framework tailored to operational constraints of industrial deployment. It translates implication‑level requirements into concrete items that can be used to analyse where current RFMs are industrially mature, where they are incomplete, and which research directions are likely necessary for credible industrial uptake. The subsequent survey section will employ this framework to discuss existing RFMs and highlight gaps between current capabilities and implication‑derived expectations.

The authors performed an iterative qualitative synthesis of 125 manually reviewed industrial works to extract recurring requirements, constraints, and deployment challenges for robotic systems. They grouped excerpts into thematic clusters, refined them into eleven compact implications, and observed that the themes are interdependent rather than contradictory, often describing the same practical challenge (e.g., human presence) from multiple angles such as safety, interaction design, robustness, or perception.

**Implication 1 – Adaptability & Flexibility**  
Across domains, variability in processes, product variants, and boundary conditions is repeatedly described as a defining property of real deployments, increasing re‑parameterisation effort and uncertainty. Traditional automation is portrayed as brittle under minor changes, whereas adaptability is framed as a key enabler for fast, low‑cost production and personalisation. Industrial environments are often dynamic, partially known, or unstructured, with unpredictable events and human presence intensifying the need for robots and control methods that can adjust behaviour online, be reconfigurable across products and processes, and reduce costly reprogramming cycles. Sector‑specific discussions (e.g., logistics, outdoor work) highlight environmental variation (lighting, weather, clutter) as a robustness requirement. Cobots’ flexible design and ease of reconfiguration are noted, but such flexibility must also be reflected in the control system, which must be intrinsically agnostic to changing tasks, embodiments, or sensor setups.

**Implication 2 – Safety & Compliance**  
Safety is consistently portrayed as a gating factor for industrial deployment, especially in shared workspaces and high‑consequence settings. Deploying cobots in shared spaces requires safety‑aware control logic that prevents injuries, satisfies certification and standards (e.g., ISO 10218, ISO/TS 15066, regional standards), and remains robust under dynamic, unpredictable conditions such as human behavioural variability and sensing uncertainty. Safety mechanisms that trigger overly conservative stops can reduce efficiency, motivating approaches that integrate safety‑aware reasoning and sensing to preserve productivity while protecting operators. The literature also stresses safe operation under realistic uncertainty, including failures and out‑of‑distribution inputs.

**Implication 3 – Human‑Robot Interaction & Collaboration (HRI & HRC)**  
A significant segment envisions future industrial robotics as inherently human‑centric, with robots and humans working in proximity or physical collaboration to combine human flexibility and cognition with robotic repeatability and precision. Interaction taxonomies (coexistence, cooperation, collaboration; remote, proximity, physical) are used to emphasise diverse interaction regimes and the need for corresponding interface and coordination solutions. Direct physical collaboration is valued for flexibility but requires perception of contact and appropriate response. Communication quality, interface usability, and natural modalities (e.g., speech) are repeatedly called for to reduce reliance on expert programming and support operators in real time. Current control and programming workflows are described as labour‑intensive, motivating approaches that allow operators to instruct, supervise, and correct systems directly. Collaborative scenarios also require reactive methods that can handle uncertainty and unexpected behaviour to maintain fluid workflows.

**Implication 4 – Robustness & Reliability**  
Industrial environments are repeatedly characterised as uncertain, noisy, and prone to disturbances and component imperfections. Both internal uncertainties (unmodelled dynamics, friction, sampling delays) and external uncertainties (measurement errors, environmental noise) are cited as persistent challenges. The literature calls for robust methodologies that integrate perception, planning, and control under uncertainty, especially in complex systems such as warehouse automation or autonomous mobility. Reliability is linked to monitoring and timely status updates to support reactive planning. Robustness is extended to resilience against faulty sensors, out‑of‑distribution inputs, and adversarial or cybersecurity threats, with expectations that systems maintain stable operation, provide meaningful status, and exhibit fault awareness.

**Implication 5 – Precision & Accuracy**  
While flexibility is emphasized, the corpus simultaneously stresses that industrial value derives from high precision, repeatability, and quality‑critical execution. Competitive advantage is framed in terms of efficiency and accuracy; many tasks require both throughput and reliable outcome quality. Accuracy is required not only for actuation but also for sensing and perception, which are treated as foundational for safe and correct operation. Gaps in grasping and positioning accuracy in demanding settings are noted, motivating improved sensing and algorithms. Vision‑language‑guided control is highlighted as needing higher precision and improved motion‑planning accuracy while retaining flexibility.

**Implication 6 – Real‑Time Performance**  
Real‑time capability is presented as a pervasive constraint affecting sensing, decision‑making, interaction, and control. Execution‑time considerations at action and task levels, low‑level real‑time communication, and motion control are cited. Real‑time sensing and processing are required to acquire environmental information and integrate multimodal signals for sudden responses and higher‑level reasoning. Computational and resource constraints, especially for edge deployment, limit data‑driven methods due to training/inference complexity. Even the most capable edge devices lag behind workstation GPUs, yet real‑time performance must still be achieved on these platforms. Real‑time planning in dynamic scenes is identified as an unresolved challenge, while smaller models are suggested as a possible path to real‑time inference.

**Implication 7 – Cost‑Effectiveness & Integration Capabilities**  
Automation must be economically justified, including for low‑volume production and SMEs. Solutions are expected to reduce manual effort, errors, and operational costs; high system cost is identified as a barrier to wider adoption of advanced autonomy. Frequent product changes increase reprogramming effort and cost, motivating approaches that reduce commissioning overhead and ease reconfiguration. Integration of state‑of‑the‑art research components into industrial systems is described as a practical obstacle due to lacking community‑wide

The authors evaluated industrial readiness for all 324 manipulation‑capable or generalist robot‑foundation models (RFMs) in their main corpus (out of 341 total publications) by applying an automated, large‑language‑model (LLM) pipeline. Each paper was checked against 149 implication‑grounded criteria, producing 48 276 criterion‑level decisions. Manual annotation at this scale was deemed infeasible, so the pipeline used GPT‑5.1 to extract evidence from the full text and to decide, for each criterion‑paper pair, whether the criterion was fulfilled. To prevent cross‑contamination, each evaluation run isolated a single criterion and a single paper via a dedicated vector store that was deleted after the decision. The LLM output included a binary judgement, a flag for direct statement, a confidence score, an evidence‑availability signal, extracted quotes (or a statement of no information), and a brief rationale. The LLM was instructed to adopt a conservative stance, marking a criterion as unfulfilled unless clearly supported, yielding intentionally cautious maturity estimates.

Reliability was assessed on three expert‑rated papers (two annotated before, one after the automated run). Table 8 shows that the LLM reproduced the expert implication‑level patterns, preserving the qualitative ranking: Gemini Robotics 1.5 > OpenVLA, while π0 remained limited. On 447 criterion‑level judgments (Table 9), the LLM achieved 0.966 accuracy, F1 = 0.762 for the positive class, Cohen’s κ = 0.744, false‑positive rate = 1.9 % and false‑negative rate = 22.6 %, reflecting the conservative policy. Filtering by the “information‑found” flag did not improve F1 or κ. Per‑paper agreement (Table 10) was high for Gemini Robotics 1.5 and OpenVLA, but lower for π0 due to its very low expert positive rate (2.7 %). Disagreements often stemmed from interpretive differences in criteria (e.g., “low‑data adaptation” thresholds) rather than outright errors. Some criteria are inherently stringent, causing the LLM to mark them unfulfilled when papers lack absolute guarantees.

Overall, the authors conclude that the pipeline provides sufficiently reliable, conservative maturity estimates for scaling assessment across hundreds of RFMs, supporting model comparison and implication‑level analysis while advising caution for fine‑grained criterion‑level interpretations due to the elevated miss rate and interpretive latitude.

Section: 7.3 Evaluating Industrial Maturity: A Criteria Catalogue
response: The authors built a living catalogue of 149 criteria—derived from 517 implication‑attribute pairs—to evaluate the industrial readiness of robotic foundation models (RFMs) and their deployment ecosystems, distinguishing model‑centric, ecosystem‑centric, and joint requirements such as adaptive behavior, documentation, and structured logging. They note intentional redundancy across implications to preserve diagnostic detail, and map each criterion to emerging research on multi‑hardware support, out‑of‑distribution robustness, confidence calibration, interactive clarification, supervisory safety layers, memory, data governance, and privacy. The catalogue thus bridges industrial expectations with current RFM capabilities, highlighting gaps that must be addressed for credible industrial uptake.

The authors synthesized eleven recurring industrial implications from 125 manually reviewed works, noting that themes are interdependent rather than contradictory and that each reflects a dominant expectation for deployed robotic systems and learning‑based control. These implications are: (1) adaptability and flexibility to handle frequent task, process, and environmental variation without extensive reprogramming; (2) safety and compliance with standards (e.g., ISO 10218, ISO/TS 15066) while maintaining operation under uncertainty and avoiding efficiency loss; (3) human‑robot interaction and collaboration requiring natural, intuitive communication, continuous operator involvement, and reactive methods for variable, partially automatable tasks; (4) robustness and reliability to sustain stable operation amid internal/external uncertainties, sensor degradation, OOD inputs, and security threats; (5) precision and accuracy in actuation and perception to meet quality‑critical, high‑throughput demands; (6) real‑time performance across sensing, decision‑making, and control despite limited compute resources; (7) cost‑effectiveness and integration capabilities that reduce commissioning overhead, support low‑volume production, and fit heterogeneous, resource‑constrained hardware; (8) explainability and trust through transparent models and interfaces that foster operator acceptance and safe collaboration; (9) sensor fusion and perception pipelines that combine multimodal data to overcome single‑sensor limitations and support safe HRC; and (10) standardized benchmarking and evaluation to provide reproducible, task‑relevant assessments, while (11) data requirements and usage emphasize scarcity, high acquisition cost, and the need for data‑efficient, continual‑learning methods. The authors argue that these implications constitute adoption bottlenecks that often prevent laboratory‑grade approaches from translating to production, and they will structure the subsequent analysis of robotic foundation models’ industrial readiness.

The authors aimed to evaluate industrial readiness of all 324 manipulation‑capable RFMs (out of 341) by applying an automated LLM‑based pipeline (GPT‑5.1) that assessed each paper against 149 implication‑grounded criteria in isolated runs, producing binary fulfilment judgments, confidence scores, evidence flags and rationales while conservatively marking unsupported criteria as unfulfilled; expert comparison on three blind‑rated papers showed high agreement (accuracy 0.966, κ 0.744) with a low false‑positive rate (1.9 %) but a higher false‑negative rate (22.6 %) reflecting the cautious policy; the authors conclude the pipeline yields reliable, lower‑bound maturity estimates suitable for corpus‑level analysis yet advise caution for individual criterion interpretations due to interpretive latitude and occasional disagreement.

enabling dimensions at a time, but do not yet

The authors examined industrial applicability of robot‑foundation models (RFMs) by analysing all 324 evaluated papers and a high‑performing Top‑50 subset. Using per‑implication industrial‑maturity scores, they presented two complementary views: (a) a temporal‑stability overview of which implications are addressed (Figure 11) and (b) a breadth‑versus‑depth analysis of coverage per implication (Figure 12, Table 13).

**Temporal‑stability overview.** Normalised per‑implication criterion‑fulfilment ratios (sum of fulfilled criteria within an implication and year divided by the number of papers published that year) were plotted for 2020‑2025. The authors report that the overall profile is “highly consistent”: the same small subset of implications dominates each year while the remaining implications stay “persistently low”. Specifically, the literature repeatedly concentrates on adaptability/flexibility (I1), benchmarking/evaluation (I10), and data requirements/usage (I11). In contrast, safety/compliance (I2), human‑robot interaction/collaboration (I3), real‑time performance (I6), and cost‑effectiveness/integration (I7) remain comparatively under‑represented. No monotonic rise is observed for any implication, leading the authors to conclude that current RFM research is not yet converging toward progressively more holistic industrial coverage; rather, the field deepens within a relatively stable set of research emphases.

**Breadth‑vs‑depth analysis.** The authors defined two metrics per implication: (1) 1+‑Coverage, the share of papers meeting at least one criterion (breadth), and (2) Average Criteria Coverage (ACC), the average fraction of criteria met per paper (depth). Figure 12 and Table 13 show a “consistent breadth‑depth mismatch”. For the full corpus, strong breadth is observed only for three implications: I1 (1+‑Coverage = 0.756), I10 (0.753), and I11 (0.707). Even for these, depth remains low: ACC values are below 0.10 (I10 = 0.099, I11 = 0.097, I1 = 0.089). Several industrially critical implications exhibit very low breadth: safety/compliance (I2 = 0.034), HRI/HRC (I3 = 0.052), real‑time performance (I6 = 0.049), and cost‑effectiveness/integration (I7 = 0.071). The Top‑50 subset shows near‑universal breadth for seven implications (I1, I4, I5, I8, I9, I10, I11 all with 1+‑Coverage = 1.0), but depth improves only modestly (e.g., I1 = 0.238, I10 = 0.232, I11 = 0.227) while remaining low for I2 (0.019), I3 (0.043), I6 (0.036), and I7 (0.050). Thus, even the strongest papers display limited multi‑criterion, implementation‑relevant coverage.

**Most frequently fulfilled criteria.** Table 14 lists the ten criteria most often satisfied across all papers. They cluster in the three dominant implications: Multi‑Task Generalisation (I1, fulfilment rate = 0.4938), Flexible Data Type Acceptance (I11, 0.4877), Repeatability & Reproducibility (I10, 0.4475), Low‑Data Adaptation & Few‑Shot Requirements (I11, 0.4198), and several benchmarking‑related criteria (I10). Explicitness of fulfilment is relatively low for Multi‑Task Generalisation (0.2812) and Repeatability & Reproducibility (0.2483), indicating that many reported fulfilments are inferred from experiments rather than directly stated. Low‑Data Adaptation shows higher explicitness (0.8088), reflecting its frequent explicit highlighting, though the authors note that interpretation latitude may inflate its fulfilment rate.

**Evidence‑fulfilled‑gap analysis.** Table 15 reports, for each implication, the criterion with the highest evidence rate, its gap score (gc = EvidRate − FulfillRate), evidence availability, and fulfilment rate. Gap scores are large for almost every implication, frequently exceeding 0.8, meaning that criteria are widely discussed or documentable yet rarely satisfied under the binary fulfilment policy. For example, I2’s top criterion (Reactive, Real‑Time Safety) has EvidRate = 0.8117 but FulfillRate = 0.0031 (gc = 0.8086); I3’s Collaborative Adaptation shows EvidRate = 0.8981, FulfillRate = 0.0247 (gc = 0.8735). Even for well‑covered implications, gaps remain (I1’s Multi‑Task Generalisation: EvidRate = 0.9938, FulfillRate = 0.4938, gc = 0.5000). The authors interpret these gaps, together with low ACC values, as evidence that the corpus increasingly acknowledges industrial constraints but typical papers still implement only limited, criterion‑incomplete solutions—particularly for deployment‑integration (I7), safety/compliance (I2), real‑time performance (I6), and HRC/HRI (I3).

Industrial robotics is shifting from isolated, highly optimised automation toward flexible, collaborative deployment where humans and robots share workspaces. This transition is driven by cobot uptake in high‑mix, low‑volume settings and SMEs, where traditional automation is often impractical because of commissioning effort, frequent production changes, and the need for specialised expertise. Modern cobots provide safe physical design, appropriate payload, sizing and low operating power, but they do not solve the central bottleneck: robust, deployment‑ready intelligence that can flexibly adapt behaviour to changing tasks, environments and multimodal input without prohibitive engineering overhead.

The authors frame robot foundation models (RFMs) as a promising enabling technology because they target multi‑task competence, cross‑domain generalisation, and instruction‑ or demonstration‑driven low‑effort reconfiguration—dimensions where classical control and specialised learning‑based approaches remain limited. However, cobot characteristics (high mechanical precision, moderate payload, low median power in the 0.5‑20 kg class) amplify demands on learning‑based control: industrial value is often limited by perception and decision‑making under real‑world variability, and RFMs must operate with low‑latency, energy‑aware inference on edge platforms rather than workstation‑grade hardware. Multi‑sensor configurations, sensor fusion and modular end‑effectors further require interface‑flexible intelligence that tolerates changing observation and action spaces.

To capture these realities, the authors distilled eleven interdependent industrial implications, extracted 47 deployment‑relevant attributes, and built an implication‑attribute matrix (11 × 47 = 517 considerations) that yielded 149 concrete criteria spanning model capabilities and ecosystem requirements. Their assessment of 324 discovered RFMs (48 276 criterion‑level decisions) shows that even top‑ranked models achieve only 0.11‑0.12 overall maturity (≈10 % of criteria met) and typically score highly on at most two or three implications. The strongest systems exhibit implication‑wise “peaks” (e.g., structured reasoning, human‑in‑the‑loop interaction) rather than balanced coverage; Gemini Robotics 1.5 leads overall and scores highest on adaptability/flexibility (I1 = 0.44) but is near zero on several deployment‑critical implications.

Across the full corpus, research consistently concentrates on adaptability/flexibility (I1), benchmarking/evaluation (I10) and data requirements/usage (I11), while safety/compliance (I2), HRI/HRC (I3), real‑time performance (I6) and cost‑effectiveness/integration (I7) remain persistently underrepresented. Even the Top‑50 subset shows modest depth for leading implications and weak breadth/depth for deployment‑critical ones. The authors conclude that current RFM progress isolates and optimises individual bottlenecks but lacks comprehensive, industry‑grade integration.

They propose concrete priorities: (1) move from isolated capability demos to layered systems with planning, memory, action generation, verification and safety gating as central, testable components; (2) bridge underrepresentation of safety/compliance, real‑time feasibility and integration by developing evaluation protocols that address low‑latency edge inference, structured logging, and handling of changing sensor/tooling interfaces; (3) leverage the strong emphasis on benchmarking to create evaluations reflecting deployment realities (distribution shifts, failure recovery, human supervision, long‑horizon operation) and to diagnose failure causes; (4) close large evidence‑fulfilment gaps by turning recognised industrial desiderata into robust implementations, documentation and validation.

In conclusion, RFMs constitute a credible pathway to unlock cobot‑centred automation, directly targeting flexibility, reconfigurability and intuitive instruction demanded by modern industrial production, especially in cost‑ and changeover‑sensitive settings. Yet the corpus‑scale evaluation demonstrates that current RFM research remains predominantly laboratory‑oriented relative to deployment‑grounded industrial requirements. The presented implication synthesis and criteria catalogue provide a transparent industrial‑readiness reference to evaluate and guide future RFMs toward auditable, safe, real‑time‑capable and integration‑ready systems, with safety/compliance, HRI/HRC, real‑time performance and cost‑effectiveness/integration identified as the central research agenda.

response: Industrial robotics is shifting toward collaborative cobot deployment, but robust, adaptable intelligence remains the bottleneck; RFMs promise multi‑task, cross‑domain, low‑effort reconfiguration yet must meet stringent safety, real‑time, integration, and cost constraints on low‑power edge hardware. An assessment of 324 models using 149 criteria shows the best RFMs satisfy only ~10 % of requirements, with strengths in adaptability but persistent gaps in safety/compliance, HRI/HRC, real‑time performance, and integration. Closing these gaps is identified as the central agenda for achieving industry‑grade autonomous cobots.

The analysis of 324 evaluated robot‑function‑modelling papers (and a Top‑50 subset) shows that industrial‑relevance coverage is temporally stable and concentrated on a few implications—adaptability/flexibility (I1), benchmarking/evaluation (I10), and data requirements/usage (I11)—while safety/compliance (I2), HRI/HRC (I3), real‑time performance (I6) and cost‑effectiveness/integration (I7) remain consistently under‑addressed; breadth (1+‑Coverage) is high only for the three dominant implications (≈0.75–0.76 in the full corpus, reaching 1.0 in the Top‑50), yet depth (Average Criteria Coverage) stays low across all implications (≤0.10 in the full set, ≤0.24 in the Top‑50), with the strongest depth again limited to I1, I10 and I11. Moreover, the ten most frequently fulfilled criteria cluster in these three implications (e.g., Multi‑Task Generalisation, Flexible Data Type Acceptance, Repeatability & Reproducibility), but explicitness of fulfilment is modest for several (e.g., 0.28 for Multi‑Task Generalisation), and gap analysis reveals large discrepancies between evidence presence and actual fulfilment (gap scores often >0.8), indicating that while the literature increasingly discusses industrial constraints, most papers implement only partial, criterion‑incomplete solutions, especially for the under‑represented implications I2, I3, I6 and I7.

correction throughout execution, enabling course correction and adjustment without

3. Multi-Task Generalisation: Handles multiple task types/categories, including unseen

goal stays primary (may autonomously adapt solution approaches/ strategies).

the commanded task goal: deviating too far from user instructions triggers feedback,
halt, or request for approval.
C. Environmental Adaptation and Robustness
6. Generalisation to Environmental Variation: Maintains consistent performance across
diverse environmental conditions (lighting, weather, background, friction, etc.),
object/material variations, and scene clutter, with minimal degradation.
7. Autonomous Handling of Distractors/Obstacles: Identifies and robustly manages/
handles unknown, distracting, or non-required objects in the scene or obstacles along
the path/ trajectory (including incorporation into task strategy if needed).
8. Online Environment Adaptation & Response: Recognises and continuously adapts to
environmental changes, such as errors, faults, sensor degradation or external influences
during operation: e.g. logging, halting, or feedback-requesting as confidence drops.
9. Autonomous Fallbacks: Capable of autonomously choosing context-appropriate
error/fault responses (e.g. request feedback, switch input modalities, logging, etc.) and
behaviour (e.g. continue operation, transition to safe state, adapt strategy, etc.)
without requiring predefined fallback behaviour.
D. Instruction and Feedback Flexibility
10. Multimodal Command Interface: Accepts user-input (task instructions,
correction/feedback, etc.) via diverse modalities (natural language in multiple
languages, images, teaching by demonstration, video, etc.).
11. Mid-Execution Feedback Responsiveness: Remains receptive to user feedback and
correction throughout execution, enabling course correction and adjustment without
re-initiating trajectories.

health, energy/ compute utilisation).

adapted behaviour and adherence to user command(s): Flags or readjusts if deviation
from expected outcome or operator intent is detected.

Implication Category/ Criterion
2. Instruction Confidence: For every operator command or query, provides a confidence
score reflecting certainty in both (a) correct recognition of the input (e.g. speech
recognition, gesture identification), and (b) correct interpretation of the operator’s
intent. When confidence is low, proactively seeks clarification or reframing from the
operator, and communicates the reason for uncertainty (ambiguity, low signal, novel
command, etc.).
3. Intuitive Feedback Acceptance: Integrates operator clarifications, corrections, or input
refinements (e.g. specifying objects, adjusting approach, clarifying intent) online, into
the ongoing action interpretation or prediction – adapting its immediate responses and
future understanding, mostly without pausing or disrupting the main task flow.
B. Responsiveness & Interaction Control
4. Real-time Interruptibility: Allows operators/ users to instantly and directly pause,
modify, query, or halt ongoing execution or task, providing full control and safe
intervention across all interfaces and modalities.
5. Continuous Responsiveness: Maintains complete HRI/HRC accessibility and
interaction throughout all operational phases (idle, executing, transitioning,
recovering), ensuring operators can always intervene, instruct, or query – never leaving
the system ”locked out” or unresponsive.
C. Operator Management, Authorisation & Privacy
6. Active Operator Exclusivity: Guarantees that only one authorised/ known operator/
user is ”active” and in control at any time. Enforces explicit, secure handover or
switching protocols, and reliably ignores unverified or distracting bystanders in both
input and output.
7. Operator Identification & Authorisation: Identifies and responds exclusively to
securely recognised and authorised personnel/ user. Actively prevents unauthorised
commands, even under disruptive or noisy conditions, and logs all identity-related
access attempts.
8. Operator Data Privacy: Encrypts and protects operator-specific data and interaction
history; permits authorised deletion or review in accordance with relevant privacy
standards. Ensures only authorised personnel can access, modify, or request deletion of
such data.
9. Learned Operator Preferences: Adapts interface layout, communication style,
behaviour, or task sequencing to individual operators/ users – learning and persisting
preferences across sessions for efficiency and comfort unless instructed otherwise.
D. Human-Robot Collaboration & Behaviour Adaptation
10. Human Presence Awareness in Workspace: Continuously senses human presence
and proximity throughout and beyond the workspace using multiple sensor modalities
(vision, audio, proximity, etc.). Dynamically adapts operation speed, safety margins,
and communication in response to detected changes (especially in cases of unexpected
entries, operator absence, etc.).
11. Collaborative Adaptation: Reactively modulates solution strategies, action plans,
and interaction traits in direct response to real-time operator feedback, demonstrations,
or correction. Behaves as an adaptive teammate, tailoring technical and social
behaviours to maximise collaboration efficiency.
12. Human-Centric Adaptation: Dynamically and autonomously adjusts behaviour,
speed, and language/output based on human presence, operator skill/preference,
perceived operator condition, task safety factors, and perceived risk.

7. Proactive, Plan-Level Safety: Safety reasoning is incorporated into high-level
planning/solution strategies (not only reactive), evaluating alternative actions and
solutions by their associated predicted safety confidence.
C. Safety Rules, Enforcement, and Supervisory Control
8. Rule-Adherence & Autonomous Rejection: The system always respects predefined
safety/behavioural rules and can autonomously reject operator goals/commands that
pose unacceptable risk (e.g. “grab knife and throw”), e.g. supervised by independently
certified controllers/modules.
9. Command Compliance with Online-Safety: System adheres strictly to operator
commands as long as safety requirements are not compromised: Command execution is
continuously monitored and suspended/modified if unacceptable risk is detected,
providing transparent feedback (to the user/ logs/ supervisor/ etc.).
10. Redundant, Independent Safety Mechanisms: Employs multiple, independent
(possibly redundant and diverse-modality) mechanisms for safety assessment and
enforcement (e.g. dual model prediction, dedicated supervisor, independent safety
layers).
11. Decoupled, Real-Time Safety Control: Safety checks and action execution operate
independently: a ”safety semaphore” or gating mechanism ensures actions are only
predicted/executed when confidence exceeds threshold.
D. Operator/User and External Interfaces
12. Authorised Operator Detection & Override: Only authorised/ recognised operators
may control safety overrides or cause safety-critical actions; interfaces securely verify
operator identity and permissions.
13. External Safety Integration: Safety outputs/signals are shareable with other
robots/systems in plant (including alarms, safe state signals, zone definitions, and
status reports).
E. Fault Detection and Recovery
14. Fault Detection & Sensing: Actively detects major faults or safety violations.
Distinguishes between sensor fault and safety/ environmental hazard and the degree of
severity.
15. Safe, Autonomous Recovery: Recovers autonomously to a safe state after detecting
major faults, safety loss, low safety-related confidence in own actions or accidents.
16. Learning from Safety Events: Continuously adapts and improves safety
confidence/logic or recovery behaviour based on feedback from operator, supervisor
modules, comparison of actual vs. predicted safety outcomes and past incidents.
F. Transparency and Logging
17. Transparent Safety Reasoning: The system can explain its safety confidence, risk
assessment, and chosen/blocked actions to operators, both live and retrospectively
(with logs/reports or upon querying).
18. Persistent Safety Logs: All safety-relevant events, decisions, adaptations, actions,
and outcomes are logged, both user-readable and for self-improvement.

and action strategies in real-time when encountering partial sensor failures,
orientation/config changes, or slightly degraded environmental conditions, striving to
maintain performance without outright task failure.

appropriate recovery behaviour, fallback routine, or adaptation strategy.

input and output modalities. When any channel degrades or fails, the system
autonomously maintains task progress through alternative modalities, adapting
detection, execution, and communication strategies to suit the current hardware,
environment, and operator constraints.

D. Learning, Feedback & Continuous Improvement
10. Adaptive Error Learning & Memorisation: Continuously learns from past faults,
errors, environmental changes, and operator feedback –memorising causes and
resolutions to improve future fault/ error detection, prediction, and recovery.
11. Online Confidence & Reliability Assessment: Continuously generates a clear
reliability confidence score for further operation, quantifying the risk and likelihood of
fault occurrence and successful execution.
E. Supervision, Oversight & Trust
12. Supervisor Oversight & Fault Review: Employs dedicated supervisor components to
monitor for faults in execution, hardware/sensor input, and operator commands,
critically evaluating instructions and requesting operator engagement for suspected
errors.
13. Logging, Explanation & Operator Guidance: Logs and communicates faults,
anomalies, and noise through varied modalities, providing operators with actionable
explanations (what/why/when/how to resolve) and performance insights for
transparency and trust.
14. Consistent & Documented Fault Handling: Ensures both fault/anomaly-detection
and response-behaviours remain reproducible and consistent across time and conditions,
with all capabilities and accepted modalities documented and evaluated.

Accuracy meet an explicit v/P&A target.
2. Outcome Logging & Failure Reasoning: Gathers/ creates and logs all available
v/P&A-relevant task execution metrics (such as velocity and, if sensor capabilities
permit, achieved precision & accuracy) after each run. If direct measurement is not
possible, the system leverages predicted values, confidence scores, or proxy indicators.
For any deviation or failure to meet specified standards, the system documents and
explains likely reasons based on the given information.
3. User-Defined Trade-offs: Supports explicit operator input for v/P&A-trade-offs (e.g.
maximising speed at the cost of precision, or vice versa if either cannot be ensured),
before or during execution and ensures system behaviour adapts accordingly.
B. Evaluation, Reporting & Confidence
4. v/P&A-Confidence Score & Explanation: For every execution, outputs a confidence
score estimating the predicted likelihood that required v/P&A will be achieved,
factoring in task, object/material, environment, and other sensor data. When low
confidence is predicted, system can explain likely causes (e.g. out-of-distribution
scenario, sensor noise, disturbances).
5. Achievable v/P&A-Proposals: Alongside the confidence score and explanation, the
system can propose and explain alternative v/P&A-combinations likely to succeed in the
given context (task, object, environment), helping users adjust requirements if needed.
6. Transparent Documentation of v/P&A Capabilities: Achievable v/P&A-combinations
for every tested task, object, and context is provided alongside the model (including
limitations, known influence factors, etc.).
